responseText: Executive recommendation Arcads should be treated as a workflow/product layer over many model vendors, not as one magic video model. Your sources support that: Arcads exposes separate products/projects/scripts/assets/voices/actors/workflows plus image, video, talking actor, B-roll, scene, preset, and ElevenLabs import endpoints; its public API lists image models, video models, talking actor models, and preset categories separately. api-openapi-summary The research digest’s core thesis is right: the moat is probably model routing, curated situations/templates, batch workflows, asset reuse, and marketer-specific presets—not a single proprietary model. source-digest The repo’s hard constraint is clean-room, modular, separable architecture rather than cloning identities or copyrighted media. README The creative direction file is also dead-on: build an editable graph/layer pipeline and never ask video models to render readable text; captions and overlays belong in Remotion/ffmpeg/post. video-creative-direction Default stack picks 48-hour demo — optimize for visible output, not vendor purity. Confidence: high. Use GPT-5.4 mini or Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite for script/hook generation, Playwright/Firecrawl + LLM extraction for product pages, GPT Image 2 / Gemini Flash Image / Luma for stills, Fal as a broker for Kling/Seedance/Wan/Grok/Veo where possible, Google Veo 3.1 Fast or Runway Gen-4.5 for hero clips, ElevenLabs or Cartesia for voice, HeyGen or Fal Kling LipSync/MuseTalk for talking clips, Deepgram/OpenAI/AssemblyAI for captions, and Remotion + ffmpeg + Sharp for deterministic composition. OpenAI’s public pricing page currently lists Sora 2 video at $0.10/s for 720p and Sora 2 Pro up to $0.70/s for 1080p, but OpenAI’s Sora 2 API docs also say the Sora 2 models are deprecated and scheduled to shut down on September 24, 2026, so use Sora only for a short-lived demo, not as an MVP dependency. OpenAI Developers+1 1-week internal tool — optimize for routing and repeatability. Confidence: high. Build the adapter layer first. Add a small asset catalog, prompt/provenance logging, a queue, per-provider health checks, and a side-by-side comparison UI. Default to Gemini Flash-Lite / GPT mini / Claude Haiku/Sonnet for planning and extraction; GPT Image 2 or Gemini Flash Image for high-control image edits; Veo 3.1 Fast, Runway, Fal Seedance/Kling/Wan for video; ElevenLabs/Cartesia for voice; Deepgram/OpenAI/AssemblyAI for transcription. Google’s pricing page lists Imagen 4 Fast at $0.02/image and Veo 3.1 Lite/Fast/Standard tiers from $0.05/s to $0.60/s depending model/resolution, and Gemini Flash-Lite is priced as a high-volume cheap model. Google AI for Developers 1-month MVP — optimize for marketer workflow, not model novelty. Confidence: medium-high. Ship a node/DAG workflow around: product ingest → brand brief → hook/script variants → persona/actor image → product/app/try-on still → I2V/B-roll → TTS → lipsync/talking actor → captions → final render → scoring. Use Runway/Veo/Fal as paid video backends, OpenAI/Gemini image models for images, ElevenLabs/Cartesia/Deepgram for audio, and Remotion/ffmpeg for final composition. Add local pre/post tools for cost control: SAM2, rembg/RMBG, Real-ESRGAN, RIFE, faster-whisper. Runway’s API currently advertises Gen-4.5, Aleph 2.0 video editing, Seedance 2.0, and GPT Image 2 access, while Luma advertises multimodal Generate/Modify endpoints with up to nine references and product/character consistency. Runway API+1 Later RTX 3090 experiments — optimize for control, not production throughput. Confidence: medium. Use ComfyUI as the local graph lab, with FLUX.1 schnell/SDXL for image generation, Wan 2.2/2.7, LTX, AnimateDiff, ControlNet/IP-Adapter/InstantID/LoRA for video/character experiments, SAM2/RVM/rembg for masks, Real-ESRGAN/RIFE for cleanup, faster-whisper/WhisperX for captions, and MuseTalk/LivePortrait/Wav2Lip/SadTalker for lipsync tests. ComfyUI’s positioning—node graph, visible parameters, remixable workflows—matches your desired architecture. Comfy FLUX.1 schnell is Apache-2.0 while FLUX.1 dev and related editing/control models are under non-commercial licensing, so do not assume every “open” FLUX workflow is commercially usable. GitHub Evidence and pricing anchors used below OpenAI currently lists GPT-family token pricing, image pricing for GPT Image 2 / GPT Image 1 Mini, video pricing for Sora 2/Sora 2 Pro, and transcription pricing; it also notes GPT Image models may require organization verification and that image generation can have latency up to two minutes and still struggle with text/consistency in some cases. OpenAI Developers+1 Anthropic lists Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku pricing, prompt caching, 50% batch pricing, Bedrock/Vertex availability, and large-context availability for current models. Claude Platform+1 Google lists Gemini, Imagen, Gemini Flash Image, TTS, and Veo 3.1 pricing, including batch discounts and “charged only on success” for Veo entries. Google AI for Developers Fal is useful as a fast prototyping broker because it exposes image/video/audio/3D models on serverless GPUs, including Kling, Seedance, Grok Imagine, Veo, Happy Horse, Wan, and lip-sync endpoints. Fal.ai+1 Replicate’s Wan collection describes Wan as open-source/open-weight video models covering text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, video editing, and native audio in newer Wan lines, with license caveats per model. Replicate xAI’s own docs currently list Grok Imagine Image at $0.02/image and Video at $0.05/s, with promotional caveats on video extension pricing. xAI Docs+1 ElevenLabs API pricing currently lists Flash/Turbo TTS at $0.05/1K characters, Multilingual v2/v3 at $0.10/1K characters, Scribe STT at $0.22/hr, realtime Scribe at $0.39/hr, voice changer at $0.12/min, and dubbing at $0.33/min. ElevenLabs Cartesia Sonic 3.5 supports 42 languages and is positioned for low-latency natural streaming TTS, but its docs also flag model/endpoint deprecations around older Sonic/voice-embedding paths, so version pinning matters. Cartesia Docs+1 Deepgram lists Nova-3/Nova-3 Multilingual, diarization, keyterm prompting, and TTS pricing; AssemblyAI lists Universal Streaming, Universal-3 Pro Streaming, Whisper Streaming, diarization, and keyterms pricing. Deepgram+1 HeyGen’s API docs list Digital Twin generation, Avatar IV/V pricing by output duration, video translation, lipsync, and avatar creation calls; Synthesia’s docs show personal avatar creation from photo or video with consent requirements and footage guidelines. HeyGen+2HeyGen+2 SAM2 supports promptable image and video segmentation; Real-ESRGAN targets general image/video restoration; RIFE targets frame interpolation; Whisper is an MIT-licensed multilingual speech recognition/translation model. GitHub+3GitHub+3GitHub+3 Remotion is built for reusable programmatic video templates, ffmpeg is the standard cross-platform audio/video conversion tool, Sharp is high-performance Node image processing, and MoviePy is an open-source Python video editing automation library. Confidence: medium. Practical vendor menu by layer LLM layer Use three tiers. Cheap tier: Gemini Flash-Lite, GPT mini/nano, Claude Haiku for extraction, translations, format expansion, and simple hook variants. Mid tier: Claude Sonnet, GPT-5.4, Gemini Flash for brand strategy, script critique, prompt rewriting, and format decomposition. Expensive tier: Claude Opus/GPT-5.5/Gemini Pro for long-context competitor analysis or final creative direction. Anthropic’s current pricing and batch/cache discounts make Claude especially attractive for long-context and cached brand briefs; Google’s batch pricing and Flash-Lite make it attractive for high-volume extraction and localization. Claude Platform+1 For local experiments on the 3090, try Qwen3/Qwen3.6, Gemma, Mistral open, and Llama-family models, but keep them as local assistants/evaluators unless they beat cloud models on your own UGC rubric. Qwen’s repo says its open-weight models are Apache 2.0; Google’s Gemma docs describe open-weight models for local/cloud deployment; Mistral lists open models including Mistral Small 4 and Mistral Large 3. GitHub+2Google AI for Developers+2 Image layer Default: GPT Image 2 for product-sensitive edits and believable UGC stills; Gemini Flash Image / Nano Banana-style routes for fast/cheap variants; Luma Modify for multi-reference character/product work; FLUX/SDXL local for drafts, stylized influencers, and cheap batches. Google’s pricing makes Gemini Flash Image and Imagen attractive for high-throughput image work; OpenAI’s guide is better for high-control edits but warns about latency and some consistency/composition limitations. Google AI for Developers+1 Video layer Default: Veo 3.1 Fast/Standard + Runway + Fal broker. Use Fal to quickly test Kling/Seedance/Wan/Grok/Hailuo-like models without hand-writing every vendor integration. Use Runway when you need consistency/editing; use Veo for high-quality hero clips and native-audio video; use Wan/Kling/Seedance for cheap drafts and B-roll. Google’s Veo docs describe 8-second 720p/1080p/4K video with native audio; Runway lists Gen-4.5 and Aleph 2.0; Fal exposes a wide cross-section of current media models. Google AI for Developers+2Runway API+2 Do not make Sora 2 the long-term default. Arcads exposes Sora2/Sora2 Pro, but OpenAI says Sora 2 API models are deprecated and shutting down on September 24, 2026. api-openapi-summary OpenAI Developers Talking actor / lipsync layer For a 48-hour demo, use HeyGen or Fal Kling LipSync/MuseTalk. For MVP, support both “stock/custom digital twin API” and “open local lipsync” modes. HeyGen gives predictable programmatic pricing and avatar/digital twin endpoints; Synthesia provides clear consent and footage guidelines; Tavus is strong if real-time conversational video becomes a feature, but for UGC ad renders it may be overkill. Synthesia+3HeyGen+3HeyGen+3 Open/local: MuseTalk first, LivePortrait second, Wav2Lip as baseline, SadTalker for stylized talking heads. Wav2Lip remains foundational, MuseTalk targets real-time high-quality lip-sync, and LivePortrait is useful for video-driven portrait motion. GitHub+2GitHub+2 Audio layer Default voice stack: ElevenLabs for quality, Cartesia for low-latency/voice-agent-style delivery, Deepgram or OpenAI/Google for cheap/common voices, and local Kokoro/Piper/XTTS only for experiments or non-premium drafts. ElevenLabs and Deepgram pricing are straightforward enough to route automatically by job type. ElevenLabs+1 Composition layer Default: Remotion for templates and overlays, ffmpeg for encoding/QC/transmuxing, Sharp/Canvas for still assets, MoviePy for quick Python prototypes. This is non-negotiable for your product: text, captions, UI screenshots, logos, and final layout should be deterministic layers, not hallucinated by a video model. video-creative-direction Remotion+2FFmpeg+2 TypeScript provider abstraction design This is the “thin waist” you want: every provider can be weird internally, but your app sees the same request/response shape. language?: string; detectLanguage?: boolean; wordTimestamps?: boolean; speakerDiarization?: boolean; keyterms?: string[]; outputFormats?: Array<"json" | "srt" | "vtt" | "txt">;}export interface TranscriptOutput extends AssetRef { kind: "caption"; text: string; language?: string; words?: Array<{ text: string; startSec: number; endSec: number; confidence?: number; speaker?: string; }>; srtUri?: string; vttUri?: string;}export interface TranslateRequest extends CommonRequest { sourceText?: string; sourceAsset?: AssetRef; sourceLanguage?: string; targetLanguage: string; preserveTiming?: boolean; styleGuide?: string; glossary?: Record<string, string>; maxCharsPerCaptionLine?: number;}export interface TranslationOutput extends AssetRef { kind: "text" | "caption"; text: string; sourceLanguage?: string; targetLanguage: string; timedSegments?: Array<{ text: string; startSec?: number; endSec?: number; }>;}export interface ComposeRenderRequest extends CommonRequest { timeline: { width: number; height: number; fps: number; durationSec: number; background?: string; layers: Array<{ id: string; asset?: AssetRef; type: "video" | "image" | "audio" | "text" | "caption" | "shape" | "effect"; startSec: number; endSec?: number; zIndex: number; transform?: { x?: number; y?: number; width?: number; height?: number; scale?: number; rotateDeg?: number; opacity?: number; }; text?: string; style?: Record<string, unknown>; effects?: Array<{ name: string; params?: Record<string, unknown> }>; }>; }; output: { format: "mp4" | "mov" | "webm" | "gif"; codec?: "h264" | "h265" | "vp9" | "prores"; bitrate?: string; includeCaptions?: boolean; burnInCaptions?: boolean; };}export interface RenderOutput extends AssetRef { kind: "video"; poster?: AssetRef; captions?: AssetRef[]; ffprobe?: Record<string, unknown>;}export interface ProviderAdapter { name: ProviderName; capabilities(): Promise<{ models: Array<{ id: string; tasks: Array< | "generateImage" | "generateVideo" | "generateSpeech" | "lipsync" | "transcribe" | "translate" | "composeRender" >; maxDurationSec?: number; resolutions?: string[]; supportsStartFrame?: boolean; supportsEndFrame?: boolean; supportsReferenceImages?: number; supportsReferenceVideos?: number; supportsAudio?: boolean; pricing?: ProviderCost; notes?: string[]; }>; }>; generateImage?(req: GenerateImageRequest): Promise<ProviderResult<ImageOutput>>; generateVideo?(req: GenerateVideoRequest): Promise<ProviderResult<VideoOutput>>; generateSpeech?(req: GenerateSpeechRequest): Promise<ProviderResult<AudioOutput>>; lipsync?(req: LipsyncRequest): Promise<ProviderResult<VideoOutput>>; transcribe?(req: TranscribeRequest): Promise<ProviderResult<TranscriptOutput>>; translate?(req: TranslateRequest): Promise<ProviderResult<TranslationOutput>>; composeRender?(req: ComposeRenderRequest): Promise<ProviderResult<RenderOutput>>;} Cost routing policy Use a draft → promote → polish policy. Do not spend premium video seconds until the script, still frame, product placement, and voice are approved. 1. Route by job class. Cheap deterministic work goes local: scraping normalization, masking, background removal, resizing, captions, overlays, render/export. Cheap generative work goes to Gemini Flash-Lite/GPT mini/Claude Haiku, Gemini Flash Image, Wan low-res, or Fal fast tiers. Premium work goes to GPT Image 2, Luma/Runway, Veo 3.1, HeyGen precision, ElevenLabs Multilingual, or Claude/GPT flagship only after a draft passes. 2. Cache aggressively. Cache by model + provider + prompt + negativePrompt + reference asset hashes + seed + dimensions + duration + provider params. Cache product extraction, brand brief, hook variants, persona sheets, TTS audio, transcripts, masks, and rendered caption layers. Never regenerate TTS/lipsync just because a caption color changed. 3. Use batching where the vendor supports it. Use OpenAI Batch for non-urgent images/video where applicable, Anthropic batch for long prompt/script jobs, and Google batch pricing for Gemini/Gemini image tasks. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google all expose batch or caching discounts in current pricing docs. OpenAI Developers+2Claude Platform+2 4. Avoid blind retries. A retry with the same prompt and same model usually burns money. Retry once with a targeted repair prompt; then switch provider/model. Example: “product logo mutated” should route to still-frame repair first, not another full video generation. 5. Use fallback chains. Script: Gemini Flash-Lite → GPT mini → Claude Sonnet for final rewrite. Product page: cache hit → Playwright/Crawl4AI → Firecrawl managed. Product image edit: local mask/upscale → GPT Image 2 → Luma/Gemini edit. Persona still: Gemini/GPT draft → Luma/Runway consistency pass → local upscale. B-roll: cheap still → Fal Wan/Seedance → Veo/Runway hero promotion. Talking actor: TTS cache → HeyGen/Fal lipsync → local MuseTalk fallback. Captions: Deepgram → OpenAI mini transcribe → faster-whisper local. Render: Remotion local → Remotion cloud/Lambda → ffmpeg fallback. 6. Put hard budgets on every workflow node. Example: heroVideo.maxCostUsd = 4.00, brollDraft.maxCostUsd = 0.80, personaSheet.maxCostUsd = 0.50, tts.maxCostUsd = 0.08, caption.maxCostUsd = 0.02. If a node hits budget, downgrade resolution/duration before asking the user. 7. Treat failed generations as billable in your economics. Even when a vendor only charges on success, retries consume time and queue slots. Your true cost is successful outputs / accepted outputs, not vendor list price. 8. Manual approval gates. Require review before: custom actor creation, voice clone, reference-motion cloning, paid ads with health/finance claims, political/public figure likenesses, and any user-uploaded person identity. Manual tests before committing to vendors Run this exact benchmark before signing anything or building deep integrations: Ten representative UGC briefs. Include skincare, SaaS app demo, fashion try-on, supplement-like but compliant product, mobile game, finance-adjacent app, boring B2B, physical product in hand, unboxing POV, and meme/brainrot variant. Five tasks per provider. For each provider, test: product logo fidelity, face consistency, hand/object interaction, app-screen readability after compositing, and motion plausibility. Talking-head torture set. Test front-facing human, side-angle human, glasses, beard, curly hair, low light, non-human mascot, cartoon seal, noisy TTS, and multilingual dubbing. Latency under parallel load. Single requests are misleading. Test 5, 20, and 50 concurrent jobs. Log queue time, generation time, failure rate, and accepted-output rate. True accepted cost. Track not “vendor price per second” but total spend / clips a human would publish. A $0.10/s model with 25% acceptance can be more expensive than a $0.40/s model with 90% acceptance. Policy and consent workflow. Test user-uploaded actor video, voice clone revocation, asset deletion, audit logs, and “where did this asset come from?” provenance. Text/caption render QA. Verify safe zones, emoji/font fallback, line wrapping, stroke/shadow, TikTok/Reels/Shorts cropping, and subtitle timing. Your own creative file already has the right rule: readable text belongs in post. video-creative-direction Vendor lifecycle risk. Sora 2’s scheduled shutdown is the warning sign. Any vendor/model that looks hot today needs an adapter boundary and migration path. OpenAI Developers Legal/IP risk around reference videos and model providers. Do not copy exact videos, identities, or copyrighted clips. Build format mechanics, not replicas. That is already part of the project’s clean-room direction. README Local RTX 3090 viability. Before investing in local video, test whether your 3090 can produce acceptable 5-second I2V clips faster/cheaper than Fal/Replicate. My expectation: local wins for masks/upscale/captions/image experiments; APIs win for polished hero video for now. Confidence: medium. Bottom line Build the product around a provider-neutral graph: product ingest→ brand brief→ hook/script variants→ persona/image refs→ product/app/try-on stills→ I2V/B-roll/talking actor→ TTS/lipsync→ captions/overlays→ final render→ scoring/analytics→ remix queue For the next build, I’d make Fal + Google Veo + Runway + OpenAI/Gemini image + ElevenLabs/Cartesia + Deepgram + Remotion/ffmpeg the practical default stack. Then add local ComfyUI/Wan/FLUX/SAM2/Whisper tooling as a cost-control and experimentation lane, not the core production dependency yet.
